posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Trading Tokens for Better Answers
posts.subtitle: Why letting a model 'think longer' at inference can beat training a bigger one
posts.summary: Test-time compute scaling keeps a model's trained weights fixed and instead spends extra computation at inference — longer reasoning chains, more sampled attempts, or structured search — to squeeze a better answer out of a hard problem. The gains concentrate on genuinely hard questions and taper off fast on easy ones, so it trades money and latency for accuracy rather than replacing the need to pick the right problems to spend it on.

slides.title: What If the Model Just... Thought Longer?
slides.body: For years, scaling meant bigger models and more training data. Test-time compute scaling is a third lever: keep the weights fixed, but let the model spend more computation at inference — more reasoning tokens, more sampled attempts, more search — to get a better answer on a hard problem.

slides.title: Train-Time Scaling Pays the Same Price for Easy and Hard Questions
slides.body: Each further jump in parameters or pretraining tokens buys progressively smaller gains, and costs an enormous, fixed amount of compute no matter how easy or hard the actual question is. A simple arithmetic question and a brutal proof get the exact same forward pass.
bullets: Pretraining scaling laws flatten: much more compute doesn't buy proportionally more capability
Inference cost per token is identical whether the question is trivial or extremely hard
A bigger model has no way to 'try harder' on just the questions that need it

slides.title: Three Ways to Spend Extra Inference Compute
slides.body: Test-time compute scaling isn't one trick — it's a family of techniques that all trade inference FLOPs for accuracy on a per-query basis.
bullets: Longer chains of thought: let the model generate more intermediate reasoning tokens before answering
Best-of-N sampling: generate N independent attempts, then select the best one
Structured search: explore a tree of partial solutions (beam search, lookahead) instead of one greedy pass

slides.title: A Verifier Turns 'More Guesses' Into 'Better Answers'
slides.body: Sampling more attempts only helps if you can tell which attempt is good. A separate verifier, or self-consistency voting across samples, scores or selects among candidates — without that step, sampling more just gives the model more ways to be wrong.
bullets: Self-consistency: sample N independent chains of thought, take the majority final answer
Process reward models score each reasoning step, not just the final answer, catching errors earlier
A weak or missing verifier caps how much best-of-N sampling can actually help

slides.title: Two Different Scaling Axes

rows: Reasoning tokens, samples, or search at inference
Every single query, roughly proportional to effort spent
Squeezing more accuracy from an already-trained model on hard problems
Also flattens — most of the gain comes from the first several extra samples or reasoning steps, then tapers

slides.title: Example: A Hard Combinatorics Problem
slides.body: Give a model one hard problem. Greedy decoding — a single attempt — can fail because one early misstep cascades through the whole chain of reasoning. Sample many independent chains of thought at higher temperature instead, extract each one's final answer, and take the majority vote: independent correct paths tend to agree with each other more often than independent wrong paths do.
bullets: Each extra sample costs roughly as many tokens as the original single attempt
The gain only shows up on problems hard enough that the model doesn't already get right every time
On a question the model already nails consistently, extra samples buy nothing

slides.title: When NOT to Reach for More Test-Time Compute
slides.body: Test-time compute scaling isn't a free upgrade — it multiplies latency and cost per query, and it only helps when failures are inconsistent rather than systematic.
bullets: If the model is confidently and consistently wrong — a real knowledge gap — more samples just vote for the same wrong answer
Latency-sensitive products (autocomplete, live chat) often can't afford many times the inference time per request
Applying it uniformly wastes compute on easy queries that gain nothing from it — routing only hard queries into the expensive path is usually smarter

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Test-time compute scaling is a third scaling axis alongside parameters and data: spend more inference compute, not more training compute, for a better answer
Three main levers: longer reasoning chains, best-of-N sampling with a verifier, and structured search over partial solutions
Gains concentrate on genuinely hard problems and taper off fast on easy ones
It trades money and latency for accuracy — routing only hard queries into the expensive path beats applying it everywhere

questions.prompt: What does 'test-time compute scaling' change, compared to traditional scaling?
options: It increases the number of model parameters
It spends more compute at inference time, with the trained model held fixed
It adds more pretraining data
It only works by fine-tuning on new data
questions.explanation: Test-time (inference-time) scaling keeps the trained weights fixed and instead spends extra compute when answering each query — more reasoning tokens, more sampled attempts, or more search.

questions.prompt: In best-of-N sampling, why does a verifier or voting step matter so much?
options: It makes the model faster
Without a way to pick the best candidate, sampling more just produces more ways to be wrong
It reduces the number of parameters needed
It removes the need for any reasoning tokens
questions.explanation: Generating N attempts only helps if you can reliably tell good attempts from bad ones — a verifier model or majority-vote consistency check is what turns 'more guesses' into 'a better answer.'

questions.prompt: When is test-time compute scaling a poor fit?
options: On a genuinely hard reasoning problem the model sometimes gets right
On an easy query the model already answers correctly every time, or in a latency-sensitive product
When a strong verifier is available
When a problem has many equally valid reasoning paths
questions.explanation: Extra inference compute only pays off when failures are inconsistent and the task is genuinely hard; on easy queries or in latency-sensitive products, it just adds cost and delay for no accuracy gain.

posts.title: Teaching AI to Build Scientific Models, Not Just Fit Them
posts.subtitle: An agent that proposes equations, then a 100,000-run simulator tells it which ones survive
posts.summary: A guest post from Anthropic's AI for Science program reframes scientific modeling as three steps — building, constraining, interpreting — and shows how LLM agents plus simulation-based inference can automate the first two while leaving the hardest step, interpretation, to scientists. The case study: rebuilding the 1951 Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model and scaling the same idea to a 124,635-cell fruit fly brain.

slides.title: Fitting a curve isn't the same as understanding a system
slides.body: In 1951, Hodgkin and Huxley waited six months for computer time, then spent three weeks solving their own neuron model by hand. The model wasn't just a fit — building it is what told them how neurons actually fire.

slides.title: Modern models have too many plausible shapes for one 'best fit' to mean anything
slides.body: As models scale — from a single neuron to a 124,635-cell fruit fly connectome — many different equations and parameter sets can fit the same data equally well. Picking one 'winner' hides that ambiguity instead of reporting it.
bullets: A single best-fit model answers 'what fits' but not 'what's actually pinned down by the data'
Hand-building doesn't scale past small systems like a single axon
The real scientific content is often in what's shared across ALL the models that fit — not in any one of them

slides.title: Three separable steps: build, constrain, interpret
slides.body: The framework splits modeling into building (choosing the equations), constraining (fitting parameters to data), and interpreting (deciding what the fitted model means). AI can now take over the first two.
bullets: Building: what is the model made of, what form do its equations take
Constraining: tune free parameters so the model matches measurements
Interpreting: ask what the fitted model implies about the real system — still mostly a human job

slides.title: Simulation-based inference replaces a hand-derived likelihood with ~100,000 dry runs
slides.body: Instead of solving for parameters analytically, simulation-based inference (SBI) runs the simulator many times with random parameter guesses, then trains a neural network to map simulation outputs back to a distribution over plausible parameters.
bullets: ~100,000 simulations trained a Hodgkin-Huxley-scale model in the case study
Once trained, inference on new data takes seconds, not weeks
Output is a full distribution, not one point — showing which parameters are well-constrained and which aren't

slides.title: An LLM agent proposes the equations themselves — and keeps several alive at once
slides.body: On top of SBI, an agent writes code for candidate models, runs them, constrains their parameters, compares outputs to data, and revises the equations. The authors argue it should return a weighted set of plausible models, not a single 'best' one.
bullets: Agent loop: propose model → simulate → constrain via SBI → compare to data → revise
In one model-building run, candidates clustered into four groups at 41%, 39%, 11%, and 9% shares
A spread like that IS the finding — it tells you the data doesn't yet distinguish between two near-equally-good structures

slides.title: Point-estimate fitting vs. agentic SBI

rows: Distribution over parameters and model structures
Agent can propose and test many candidate structures in parallel
Explicit — shows what's constrained vs. underdetermined
Seconds, once the SBI network is trained

slides.title: Worked case: the fourth-power term that predicted a real protein structure
slides.body: Hodgkin and Huxley's equations included a term raised to the fourth power, which implied a gate made of four moving parts. Decades later, structural biology confirmed the related potassium channel is built from four identical subunits — the model's shape predicted real molecular structure.
bullets: The same logic now runs on scales Hodgkin and Huxley never had: the fruit fly connectome spans 124,635 cells
A human brain has tens of billions of neurons — hand-building at that scale isn't an option, agentic model-building might be

slides.title: Where this breaks: it's only been tested on problems we already solved
slides.body: The authors are explicit: agentic model-building has mostly been validated by rediscovering known models like Hodgkin-Huxley's. There's little evidence yet for genuinely unsolved problems, and interpretation — the step that gave Hodgkin and Huxley their Nobel Prize — still resists automation.
bullets: Rediscovery success doesn't guarantee discovery success on open questions
Interpretation isn't just a report-out step — building the model IS how scientists form understanding
Treating one AI-generated model as 'the answer' defeats the purpose; the distribution is the result

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Split modeling into building, constraining, and interpreting — AI is strongest on the first two
Simulation-based inference trades an analytical likelihood for ~100K simulations and a trained network, returning a full parameter distribution instead of one number
Let agents propose multiple competing model structures; a 41/39/11/9 split is information, not noise
This has only been proven on rediscovery so far — treat agentic model-building on genuinely open problems as unproven

questions.prompt: What does simulation-based inference (SBI) output, instead of a single best-fit parameter set?
options: A compiled binary of the simulator
A distribution over plausible parameters, showing what's constrained and what isn't
A single p-value for the whole model
A ranked list of unrelated models with no parameters
questions.explanation: SBI trains a neural network on many (~100,000 in this case) simulations to map outputs back to a distribution over parameters — the spread of that distribution is itself the scientific signal about what the data does and doesn't pin down.

questions.prompt: In the three-step framework (building, constraining, interpreting), which step do the authors say resists automation the most?
options: Building — choosing the equations
Constraining — fitting parameters to data
Interpreting — deciding what the fitted model means
None of them; all three are fully automated today
questions.explanation: The authors argue interpretation is hardest to delegate because the act of building and wrestling with a model is itself how scientists gain understanding — it's not just a final report-out step.

questions.prompt: Why does a 41%/39%/11%/9% split across four candidate models matter?
options: It means the experiment failed and should be discarded
It shows the data doesn't yet clearly distinguish between two near-equally-plausible model structures
It proves the top model (41%) is definitely correct
It's an artifact of a bug in the simulator
questions.explanation: A near-even split between the top two clusters (41% and 39%) signals genuine ambiguity in what the current data supports — exactly the kind of uncertainty a single best-fit model would have hidden.

posts.title: RLHF vs. DPO: Two Ways to Teach a Model Human Preferences
posts.subtitle: One trains a reward model and runs reinforcement learning; the other skips both
posts.summary: RLHF and DPO are the two dominant ways to turn a pile of human preference comparisons into a more helpful, aligned model. RLHF trains a separate reward model and optimizes against it with reinforcement learning; DPO collapses that into a single supervised-style loss. Same goal, very different cost and failure modes.

slides.title: A model that predicts the next token isn't the same as a model that's helpful
slides.body: Pretraining teaches a model to continue text. Getting it to follow instructions, refuse harmful requests, and prefer better answers over worse ones needs a second stage trained on human preferences.

slides.title: You can't write a loss function for 'good answer' — but humans can compare two answers
slides.body: There's no simple formula for quality, but people are reliably good at picking the better of two responses to the same prompt. Both RLHF and DPO start from the same raw material: pairs of (chosen, rejected) responses.
bullets: Raw material: thousands to millions of pairwise human preference comparisons
Goal: push the model's outputs toward 'chosen' and away from 'rejected' — without forgetting what it already knows

slides.title: RLHF: reward model + reinforcement learning, in three stages
slides.body: RLHF (used to build InstructGPT-style assistants) runs supervised fine-tuning, then trains a separate reward model on the preference pairs, then uses RL (typically PPO) to optimize the policy against that reward model.
bullets: Stage 1: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on demonstration data
Stage 2: train a reward model to score (prompt, response) pairs using the preference pairs
Stage 3: PPO samples responses from the policy, scores them with the reward model, and updates the policy to raise the score — with a KL penalty that keeps it from drifting too far from the SFT model

slides.title: DPO: the same goal, collapsed into one loss, no reward model or rollouts
slides.body: Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) uses a closed-form relationship between a reward function and the optimal policy under it. That lets you write a single classification-style loss directly on the policy, trained offline on the fixed preference pairs.
bullets: No separate reward model to train, store, or keep in sync
No online sampling/rollouts — it's a supervised pass over a static dataset, like fine-tuning
The implicit reward and the KL constraint are baked into the same loss term, instead of being three separate stages

slides.title: RLHF vs. DPO

rows: No — folded into the policy loss
Offline: one supervised pass over fixed pairs
Higher — reward model + rollouts + PPO tuning
More stable, closer to standard supervised training
Yes — reward model can rescue new rollouts
Harder — bound to the fixed preference dataset

slides.title: Worked scenario: 10,000 preference pairs, two different paths
slides.body: Say you've collected 10,000 (chosen, rejected) response pairs for a support chatbot.
bullets: RLHF path: train a reward model on the 10,000 pairs → run PPO, generating new rollouts from the live policy and scoring them with that reward model, over many iterations
DPO path: directly minimize a classification loss over the same 10,000 pairs in roughly one fine-tuning-style pass — no rollouts, no separate model to maintain
If you later collect 2,000 more pairs, RLHF's reward model can simply be retrained and PPO continues; DPO typically needs a fresh training pass over the combined dataset

slides.title: Where each one breaks
slides.body: Both approaches have real failure modes — the choice isn't free.
bullets: RLHF risk — reward hacking: the policy learns to exploit quirks of the reward model (e.g. padding answers to seem more 'thorough') instead of genuinely improving
RLHF cost — PPO is notoriously finicky to tune and needs a live sampling loop, which is expensive at scale
DPO risk — it's only as good as the fixed offline dataset; it can't explore responses outside what the preference pairs already cover
DPO limit — because there's no live reward model, it's harder to course-correct mid-training when new failure modes show up

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Both start from the same input: pairwise human preference comparisons
RLHF = SFT → reward model → PPO (online, flexible, expensive, harder to stabilize)
DPO = one offline loss that implicitly encodes the reward and the KL constraint (cheaper, more stable, bound to its dataset)
Pick RLHF when you need to keep adapting to fresh feedback; pick DPO when you have a solid fixed preference dataset and want a simpler, cheaper pipeline

questions.prompt: What does RLHF require that DPO does not?
options: Any human preference data at all
A separate reward model trained and used during an online reinforcement learning loop
A pretrained base model
A KL penalty of any kind
questions.explanation: RLHF's defining extra step is training a standalone reward model and then running PPO rollouts against it. DPO folds the equivalent of a reward signal directly into a single offline loss, so it never needs a separate reward model or live sampling.

questions.prompt: What is 'reward hacking' in the context of RLHF?
options: A security exploit that steals the reward model's weights
The policy learning to exploit quirks of the reward model (e.g., length, tone) rather than genuinely improving
A bug where the reward model returns negative numbers
Running PPO without a KL penalty
questions.explanation: Because the policy is optimized against a learned proxy (the reward model) rather than true human judgment, it can find outputs that score well on the proxy without actually being better — the classic Goodhart's-law failure of RLHF.

questions.prompt: If you need to incorporate a fresh batch of human feedback mid-training with minimal pipeline changes, which approach adapts more naturally?
options: DPO, because it has no fixed dataset
RLHF, because its reward model can be updated and PPO can keep sampling against it
Neither — both require starting over from pretraining
DPO, because PPO is required for any update
questions.explanation: RLHF's online loop (reward model + PPO rollouts) is built to keep adapting as the policy changes or as new feedback arrives. DPO is a one-shot offline fit to a fixed dataset, so folding in new feedback usually means re-running training over the combined pairs.

references.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model (Rafailov et al., 2023)

posts.title: Claude's Agent Swarm Cracked Two Black Hole Puzzles
posts.subtitle: Thousands of diagrams, checked twice, by copies of the same model.
posts.summary: Anthropic set swarms of Claude agents loose on 22 open problems in black hole physics and the bootstrap method; two produced genuine results. One settled a 20-year-old question about whether a thermal phase transition is abrupt or smooth at weak coupling, finishing a three-loop calculation spanning thousands of Feynman diagrams. The other proved an exact bound (≈9.1266) on how light the lightest 3D black hole can be, formally checked in the Lean proof assistant.

slides.title: 22 Problems In, Two Real Results Out
slides.body: Anthropic researcher Hongbin Chen asked Claude for open problems in black hole physics and the modular bootstrap, as a side test. Claude proposed 22 candidates; separate agents spent about six weeks chasing each one.
bullets: Only two produced results worth publishing — and both were independently reproduced by other agents or physicists using different methods
Neither result describes our actual universe; this is formal physics on idealized theories, not an engineering payoff

slides.title: Problem 1: Does the Thermal Transition Snap or Slide?
slides.body: In N=4 super Yang-Mills at weak coupling, gravity's gas-to-black-hole picture goes blurry. Whether the thermal transition from graviton gas to black hole is abrupt or smooth hinges on a single coefficient buried three loops deep.
bullets: Sundborg (1999), then Aharony, Marsano, Minwalla, Papadodimas, and Van Raamsdonk, showed a transition exists at all
In 2003 the same group traced the answer to one three-loop number — a calculation spanning many thousands of Feynman diagrams that was never finished for N=4
A simpler cousin theory was completed in 2005 and showed an abrupt transition; the real N=4 case stayed open for roughly two decades

slides.title: The Method: Compute Everything Twice, By Different Agents
slides.body: Claude ran as a swarm, not a single pass. Nearly every diagram was computed independently by two separate agent instances and cross-checked, with pieces also verified against known literature results and divergences tamed by hand.
bullets: Result: the transition is abrupt, even at weak coupling — combined with the known strong-coupling behavior, 'abrupt everywhere' is now the most natural picture across all couplings
The intermediate-coupling regime was not shown directly; the claim bridges the two known endpoints rather than proving the full range
A physicist who tackled the same problem independently reached the same answer by a different method — an outside check that it wasn't a shared blind spot

slides.title: Problem 2: Squeezing a 20-Year-Old Bound
slides.body: The modular bootstrap limits how light the lightest black hole in 3D AdS gravity can be: mass M1 <= c/Lambda, where c is the theory's central charge. Each tightening of Lambda took years.

rows: Proved optimal for this method; verified in Lean

slides.title: How Claude Found the Jump From 8.5 to 9.1266
slides.body: Claude noticed a pattern in numerical bootstrap data that physicists had missed, then borrowed a 'spectral curve' technique from unrelated math and physics to work out the bound's large-c behavior exactly.
bullets: An earlier Claude agent had already failed at this exact problem — 61 parallel attempts, no result
A related sphere-packing argument reproduced a bound an OpenAI model had proved separately; about half of Claude's final proof follows that same strategy
Two other independent agents landed on the identical answer, and the full result was formally checked in the Lean proof assistant in September 2026

slides.title: What This Isn't
slides.body: Anthropic is explicit about the ceiling on both results — this is a contribution to formal methods, not a physics discovery about reality.
bullets: Neither result describes our universe or has any practical application — both live in idealized, simplified gravity theories
Neither identifies the correct theory of quantum gravity
The bootstrap bound here can't by itself reach c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear — other ingredients are still needed
The version studied ignores black hole spin; other spacetime configurations (fixed energy, fixed charge) weren't analyzed

slides.title: Verification, Not Inspiration, Made This Work
slides.body: The headline isn't 'AI does physics' — it's that redundant, cross-checked agent computation let a 20-year-old three-loop calculation and a bootstrap bound both get finished.
bullets: Both results relied on independent agents reaching the same answer by different routes — the check mattered as much as the compute
One proof was formally verified in Lean rather than trusted on inspection
22 problems were attempted; 2 produced results — roughly a 9% hit rate, even with weeks of agent time per problem

questions.prompt: What ultimately resolved whether the Hawking-Page transition is abrupt or smooth at weak coupling in N=4 super Yang-Mills?
options: A new particle-collider experiment
A thousands-of-diagrams three-loop calculation, computed twice by independent Claude agents and checked against the literature
A proof that the theory has no transition at all
Running the calculation on a quantum computer
questions.explanation: The answer hinged on a single coefficient three loops deep, requiring many thousands of Feynman diagrams — Claude agents computed nearly every piece twice, independently, to catch errors.

questions.prompt: What does the modular bootstrap bound M1 <= c/Lambda actually constrain?
options: The total number of particles a theory can contain
How light the lightest black hole in 3D AdS gravity can be, relative to the theory's central charge c
The speed of light inside the theory
The number of spacetime dimensions a theory can have
questions.explanation: The bootstrap bound says any consistent 3D AdS gravity theory can't have a black hole lighter than c/Lambda — tightening Lambda rules out more candidate theories.

questions.prompt: Why does Anthropic stress that neither result 'describes our universe'?
options: Because the results were later found to be wrong
Because both are formal results about idealized theories (super Yang-Mills, pure 3D gravity), not models of real-world physics
Because Claude refused to work on realistic physics problems
Because the preprints were retracted after publication
questions.explanation: Both problems live in simplified, non-realistic theories used to stress-test gravity's mathematical structure — valuable for the bootstrap program, but not a claim about physics of the actual universe.

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Guessing Ahead to Decode Faster
posts.subtitle: A cheap draft model guesses; the big model just checks its work.
posts.summary: LLM decoding generates one token per sequential forward pass, leaving most of a GPU's compute idle since each step is memory-bandwidth bound. Speculative decoding fixes this by having a cheap draft model guess several tokens ahead, then having the full model verify all of them in a single parallel pass — accepting the matching prefix and correcting only the first wrong guess, with zero change to output quality.

slides.title: Autoregressive Decoding Wastes Your GPU
slides.body: Generating text token by token is inherently sequential: the model can't write token N+1 until it has produced token N. Each step is one tiny matrix multiply — bottlenecked on reading weights from memory, not on raw compute.
bullets: A single decode step uses only a sliver of a GPU's available FLOPs because it's memory-bandwidth bound, not compute-bound
Speculative decoding doesn't make one token cheaper — it checks several tokens in the same forward pass

slides.title: One Forward Pass, One Token — Every Time
slides.body: Standard decoding runs a full forward pass to produce exactly one new token, then repeats. Latency scales linearly with output length, and most of each pass is spent moving weights, not computing.
bullets: Batching raises throughput but doesn't help single-request latency — a chat reply still takes one sequential pass per token
Bigger models make every one of those passes more expensive, so decode latency grows directly with model size
The GPU has spare compute during decode precisely because the step is memory-bound — that idle capacity is the opportunity

slides.title: Draft Cheap, Verify in Parallel
slides.body: A small, fast 'draft' model proposes several tokens in a row. The big 'target' model then checks all of those draft tokens in a single forward pass — roughly the same cost as checking one token, since the extra tokens are batched together.
bullets: The target model accepts every draft token that matches what it would have generated itself, left to right
At the first mismatch, it rejects the remaining guesses and supplies its own correct token instead
This uses rejection sampling, so the output distribution is mathematically identical to standard decoding — no quality loss, only fewer sequential steps

slides.title: A Worked Example: 4 Guesses, 3 Keepers
slides.body: The target model is generating 'The capital of France is Paris, the'. A draft model proposes 4 tokens ahead: 'Paris', ',', 'the', 'city'. The target checks all 4 in one pass.
bullets: Tokens 1-3 ('Paris', ',', 'the') match what the target would have picked on its own — all three are accepted for free
Token 4 ('city') doesn't match; the target's own next token ('capital') is substituted instead
Net result: 4 tokens advanced for roughly the price of one target forward pass, instead of 4 separate sequential ones

slides.title: Where the Speedup Actually Comes From
slides.body: Published speculative decoding work (Leviathan et al.'s original method, plus later approaches like Medusa and EAGLE) reports real wall-clock speedups with identical output quality, though the exact multiplier is workload- and model-dependent.

rows: Roughly 2-3x on many LLM workloads; higher when the draft model predicts well
Smaller gains, but no separate draft model to maintain

slides.title: When the Trick Doesn't Pay Off
slides.body: Speculative decoding only wins when the draft model is cheap AND predicts the target well — both conditions can fail.
bullets: If the draft model's guesses rarely match the target, you pay for wasted draft generation and gain little — acceptance rate drives the entire speedup
At large batch sizes, decoding is already compute-bound rather than memory-bound, so there's less idle GPU capacity left to exploit
It needs a draft model that's both fast and aligned with the target's distribution — building or maintaining a good one is real engineering work
Hosting the draft model alongside the target model costs extra GPU memory

slides.title: Spend Idle Compute to Buy Back Latency
slides.body: Speculative decoding turns decode's usually-wasted compute into fewer sequential steps, with zero change to output quality.
bullets: Core idea: draft several tokens cheaply, verify them all in one parallel pass, accept the matching prefix
Speedup is driven by the draft model's acceptance rate, not by shrinking the target model
It's a serving-time optimization orthogonal to quantization, batching, and KV-cache tricks — and is often combined with them

questions.prompt: Why is standard autoregressive LLM decoding inefficient on GPUs?
options: It uses too much disk space
Each step produces only one token and is bottlenecked on memory bandwidth, leaving GPU compute mostly idle
It requires retraining the model after every token
It only runs on CPUs, not GPUs
questions.explanation: A single decode step is one tiny matmul per token — the GPU spends most of its time moving weights from memory rather than computing, so a lot of compute capacity sits unused.

questions.prompt: In speculative decoding, what happens when a draft model's guessed token doesn't match what the target model would have produced?
options: The entire generation restarts from scratch
The target model keeps the draft token anyway to save time
The target model rejects that token and every guess after it, and supplies its own correct token instead
The draft model is permanently discarded and never used again
questions.explanation: Verification is sequential within the draft window: every draft token up to the first mismatch is accepted, the mismatched one is replaced by the target's own choice, and the remaining guesses in that round are dropped.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't speculative decoding change the quality of the generated output?
options: It only works when the draft model is identical to the target model
It uses a rejection-sampling scheme that guarantees the same output distribution as decoding from the target model alone
It regenerates the output a second time to double-check it
It lowers the sampling temperature to make outputs more deterministic
questions.explanation: The accept/reject rule is designed so the net result is mathematically equivalent to sampling from the target model one token at a time — speculation changes how many sequential steps that takes, not what gets sampled.

posts.title: vLLM 0.34 Lets the KV Cache Size Itself After Boot
posts.subtitle: Memory is measured after warmup, not guessed before it.
posts.summary: vLLM 0.34 turns on 'extensible KV cache' by default, sizing the cache from memory that is actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup instead of a conservative pre-warmup estimate. On MiniMax-M3 on H200 that grew usable KV cache from 433k to 672k tokens, at the cost of 6-18% higher per-token decode latency at high concurrency.

slides.title: The KV Cache Now Grows Into Whatever Memory Is Left
slides.body: vLLM 0.34, released November 16, flips on 'extensible KV cache' by default: the cache is sized from memory that is actually free after warmup, not a cautious estimate made before the model ever ran.
bullets: On MiniMax-M3 on H200, usable KV cache capacity grew from 433k to 672k tokens — a ~55% jump with zero hardware change
The release ships 1,061 commits from 412 contributors and adds 10 new supported models, including Mistral Large 4

slides.title: Old Sizing Left Real Memory on the Table
slides.body: Before this release, vLLM sized the KV cache from an estimate of free GPU memory computed before CUDA graphs were captured and before warmup ran — a conservative number that didn't reflect what was actually available once the server was live.
bullets: CUDA graph capture and warmup both consume and then release memory in ways a pre-warmup estimate can't see
That gap meant servers were running with smaller max-context and lower concurrency than the hardware actually supported
The fix required either overriding --gpu-memory-utilization by hand per model, or just losing the free capacity

slides.title: Measure After Warmup, Not Before
slides.body: Extensible KV cache defers sizing until after the model has actually finished its startup sequence, then allocates the cache from whatever memory is genuinely free at that point.
bullets: Sequence: load weights -> capture CUDA graphs -> run warmup -> measure real free memory -> size the KV cache pool
On by default in 0.34; it's a sizing-time change, not a new data structure, so existing serving code and APIs are unaffected
Two escape hatches ship alongside it: a fixed --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9, or fully opting out with --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache

slides.title: More Context Capacity, Slightly Slower Decode
slides.body: The gain isn't free: packing more tokens into the same GPU means more contention for memory bandwidth during decode.

slides.title: A Team Serving MiniMax-M3 Gets Headroom They Didn't Ask For
slides.body: A platform team running MiniMax-M3 on a fixed H200 fleet upgrades to 0.34 and, without changing any config, can now hold 55% more concurrent context per GPU — meaning fewer requests get rejected for exceeding max context during traffic spikes.
bullets: Under light load, nothing changes for end users — just more headroom sitting idle
Under concurrency 128+, p50 latency per generated token creeps up 6-18%; a latency-sensitive chat product notices this in its dashboards
The team pins --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 on their latency-critical pool and leaves extensible KV cache on for their batch/throughput pool

slides.title: When Not to Take the Default
slides.body: Extensible KV cache trades a latency tax for capacity headroom — the right call only if capacity, not tail latency, is your bottleneck.
bullets: Skip it (use --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache) for strict low-latency SLAs where even an 18% TPOT bump at high concurrency breaks a budget
Skip it if you already tune --gpu-memory-utilization precisely per model — the new default sizing can shift your known-good headroom
Remember the block-size default also moved from 16 to 64; pass --block-size 16 explicitly if your deployment depends on the old value
ROCm users on versions below 10.0 can't take this release at all — ROCm 7.2 support was dropped

slides.title: Capacity You Didn't Have to Ask For — With a Catch
slides.body: vLLM 0.34 reclaims memory that static pre-warmup estimates were leaving unused, turning it into extra KV cache capacity by default.
bullets: +~55% KV cache tokens on MiniMax-M3/H200 in the release's own example, for +6-18% decode latency at high concurrency
Two flags let you opt out per-deployment: --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache
Check the breaking changes before upgrading: block-size default (16->64), ROCm 10.0 requirement, huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0

questions.prompt: What changed in how vLLM 0.34 sizes the KV cache by default?
options: It now uses a fixed cache size for every GPU model
It measures free memory after CUDA graph capture and warmup, instead of estimating before them
It moves the KV cache entirely to CPU RAM
It removes the KV cache and recomputes attention every step
questions.explanation: Extensible KV cache defers sizing until after warmup and graph capture finish, so it allocates from memory that is genuinely free rather than a conservative pre-warmup guess.

questions.prompt: On MiniMax-M3 on H200, what was the tradeoff of the new default at concurrency 128?
options: KV cache capacity dropped 55% but latency improved
KV cache capacity grew from 433k to 672k tokens, but per-token decode latency rose 6-18%
Throughput and latency both improved with no downside
The model stopped supporting long context entirely
questions.explanation: The release notes report a capacity gain (433k -> 672k tokens) paired with a 6-18% TPOT increase on some H200 models at concurrency 128 — more room, slightly slower per token under load.

questions.prompt: A team needs the old, more conservative KV cache sizing back for a strict-latency deployment. What should they do?
options: Downgrade GPU drivers
Pass --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache
Switch the block size to 64
There is no way to disable it
questions.explanation: vLLM 0.34 ships explicit opt-outs for the new default: a fixed memory-utilization target, or fully disabling extensible KV cache.

posts.title: LoRA: Fine-Tuning Giant Models by Training a Sliver of Them
posts.subtitle: Freeze the model, train two tiny matrices instead.
posts.summary: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes a pretrained model's weights and trains only a pair of small low-rank matrices inserted into each layer. For GPT-3 175B, the original paper reports roughly 10,000x fewer trainable parameters and 3x less GPU memory than full fine-tuning, with no added inference latency once the adapter is merged.

slides.title: Why Retrain 175 Billion Parameters to Teach a Model One New Skill?
slides.body: LoRA's answer: don't. Freeze every original weight and train a tiny low-rank add-on instead — on GPT-3 175B the paper reports about 10,000x fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning.
bullets: Same technique scales down to small models too — it's a general recipe for adapting any large pretrained network cheaply
Multiple LoRA adapters can target the same base model, each a few megabytes instead of a full multi-hundred-gigabyte checkpoint

slides.title: Full Fine-Tuning Means a Full Copy, Per Task
slides.body: Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which means storing a full optimizer state (gradients + momentum) sized to the entire model — and a brand-new full checkpoint for every downstream task you adapt it to.
bullets: For a 175B-parameter model, the optimizer state alone can dwarf the weights themselves in memory
Ten fine-tuned variants of the same base model means ten full-sized checkpoints to store and serve
Switching between tasks at serving time means swapping an entire multi-hundred-gigabyte model in and out

slides.title: Inject a Low-Rank Detour Around Each Weight Matrix
slides.body: For a frozen pretrained weight matrix W, LoRA adds a trainable update ΔW = B·A, where A and B are small matrices of rank r (often 4-64) — far smaller than W's own dimensions.
bullets: Only A and B are trained; W itself never moves, so pretrained knowledge stays intact by construction
The update is scaled by alpha/r and added to W's output: fewer parameters to learn, but the same output dimensions
Typically applied to the attention projection matrices (query/value), where the authors found the biggest gains per parameter spent

slides.title: Full Fine-Tuning vs. LoRA, on GPT-3 175B

rows: a few MB (just A and B)
none — W + BA collapses back into one matrix

slides.title: One Base Model, a Dozen Customers, a Dozen Adapters
slides.body: A platform serving fine-tuned variants for a dozen enterprise customers keeps exactly one copy of the base model loaded in GPU memory, then swaps in a customer-specific LoRA adapter — a few megabytes each — per request.
bullets: Storage cost: a dozen multi-hundred-GB full checkpoints becomes one base model plus a dozen tiny adapter files
Switching customers at request time becomes a lightweight weight-add instead of a full model reload
New customer onboarding means training a new adapter against the frozen base, not a full retraining run

slides.title: Where LoRA Falls Short
slides.body: Low-rank updates are an approximation, not a free lunch — the rank you pick is a real tradeoff.
bullets: Too small a rank underfits tasks that need a large shift from the base model's behavior (e.g., a big domain or language shift)
If adapters aren't merged into W before serving, you pay a small extra matrix-multiply at inference — negligible for one adapter, additive if you stack many
LoRA adapts behavior within what the base model already knows; it's not a substitute for pretraining when the base model lacks the underlying knowledge entirely
Picking which layers to adapt (just attention? also MLP blocks?) and the alpha/r scaling ratio both need tuning per task

slides.title: Freeze the Giant, Train the Sliver
slides.body: LoRA's core move — freeze pretrained weights, train a small low-rank add-on — turns fine-tuning from a full-model problem into a few-megabyte problem.
bullets: ~10,000x fewer trainable parameters and ~3x less training memory than full fine-tuning on GPT-3 175B, per the original paper
Merged adapters add zero inference latency; unmerged ones add a small, stackable cost
Pick rank r and target layers based on how far the task pulls from the base model's existing behavior

questions.prompt: What does LoRA actually train?
options: Every weight in the original model, at a lower learning rate
A pair of small low-rank matrices (A and B) added to selected weight matrices, while the original weights stay frozen
A separate small model that post-processes the output
Only the embedding layer
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes the pretrained weight matrix W and learns a low-rank update ΔW = B·A on top of it — the original weights never change.

questions.prompt: Why does a merged LoRA adapter add no extra inference latency?
options: Because the adapter runs on a separate GPU in parallel
Because B·A can be added directly into W, collapsing back into a single matrix of the original size
Because LoRA removes layers from the model entirely
Because inference always uses the frozen weights and ignores the adapter
questions.explanation: Once training is done, W + B·A is just another matrix of the same shape as W — there's no separate computation left to run at serving time.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of picking too small a rank r for a LoRA adapter?
options: Training becomes slower than full fine-tuning
The adapter can underfit tasks that need a large behavioral shift from the base model
The base model's weights get corrupted
Inference latency increases sharply
questions.explanation: Rank r caps how much the update matrix can express; too small a rank limits how far the adapted behavior can move from the frozen base model.

posts.title: Claude Beat the Best Published Quantum Circuits—All Eight
posts.subtitle: In one case, by 17x fewer gates.
posts.summary: Anthropic set Claude loose on eight quantum-circuit design tasks with only a one-paragraph brief and an automated evaluator per task. Working in a closed loop of propose-score-revise, it beat the best published designs on all eight, including a 17x gate reduction on the elliptic-curve benchmark used in quantum discrete-log attacks, by swapping in reversible algorithms it derived and formally verified itself.

slides.title: Claude Beat the Best Published Quantum Circuits
slides.body: Anthropic, Harvard, and QuEra gave Claude Mythos 5 plain-language specs for eight circuit-design problems plus an automated scorer. No human touched the circuits between rounds.
bullets: Tasks span chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing
Scored by qubits x gates — the two resources that decide whether a circuit is buildable at all
Led by Anthropic STEM Fellow Andi Gu with Harvard's Susanne Yelin and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard/QuEra)

slides.title: The Bottleneck: Modular Inversion Eats the Qubit Budget
slides.body: Elliptic-curve point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms that attack elliptic-curve cryptography — a standard benchmark. Its costliest step is modular inversion.
bullets: The classical fix, divsteps, isn't reversible as written — quantum circuits must be reversible
Naive reversibility means storing a full history of every branch choice made along the way
That storage cost is exactly what inflates qubit counts in prior designs

slides.title: Claude's Fix: Decode the History Instead of Storing It
slides.body: Rather than keeping a record of every branching decision, Claude found a way to reconstruct that history mathematically from the numbers left after each step.
bullets: Simple decoding rules worked at small sizes but failed at the real 256-bit target size
Claude proved new algebraic identities, derived a working decoding formula, and checked it with large-scale numerical simulation
It then formalized the correctness claim as a proof in Lean, a formal proof language

slides.title: Same Trick, Second Circuit: Swapping the Decoding Algorithm
slides.body: For the Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) optimization task, the costly step is a Reed-Solomon decoder. Claude swapped algorithms rather than just tuning the existing one.
bullets: Replaced the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp-Massey decoding, which runs the same fixed steps every round — far easier to implement as a predictable quantum circuit
A naive reversible version of that decoder would need up to 840 qubits; Claude's design uses only 19 extra qubits by reconstructing temporary values instead of storing them
Ran 403 million simulated decodings; about 1 in 10,000 fails, which Anthropic says is within the allowed error budget

slides.title: The Numbers, Side by Side
53 Hours, One Paragraph, Zero Mid-Run Human Input
slides.body: The elliptic-curve result came from a closed loop: Claude proposes a circuit in Python, an automated evaluator checks correctness and scores resource use, Claude revises — repeat.
bullets: Humans wrote one paragraph per task as the brief and built the evaluator — that's it until the end
Occasional nudges to try a qualitatively different approach were the only intervention — needed because Claude defaulted to well-known methods and over-checked results that were already correct
Total elapsed time for the elliptic-curve circuit: about 53 hours of autonomous iteration

slides.title: What This Isn't (Yet)
slides.body: Every number here comes from simulation, not a physical quantum computer.
bullets: Anthropic reports no hardware runs — gate and qubit counts are simulator estimates, so experimental validation is still the next step
The DQI decoder's 1-in-10,000 failure rate is a real tradeoff, not a rounding error, even though it's within tolerance
Circuit design is one layer of a useful quantum computer — error correction, decoders, and control hardware still have to catch up

slides.title: Smarter Algorithms Can Beat Bigger Hardware
slides.body: The historical analogue: the estimated cost of one key quantum-chemistry calculation (FeMoco) fell from about 50 trillion Toffoli gates (2017) to about 340 million (2025) — roughly 150,000x — almost entirely from circuit redesign, not better chips.
bullets: Claude's results fit that same pattern: cheaper quantum computing by rethinking the algorithm, not just scaling qubits
An AI that can propose, simulate, and formally verify its own circuit designs changes who can do this kind of optimization
Full technical paper: arXiv 2610.22367

questions.prompt: What let Claude make the modular-inversion circuit reversible without storing a full history of branch choices?
options: It added a classical ancilla register for every step
It derived a formula to decode the branch history directly from the resulting numbers
It skipped reversibility by measuring mid-circuit
It used Shor's algorithm instead of divsteps
questions.explanation: Claude proved new algebraic identities that let it reconstruct ('decode') the branch history from the numbers left after each iteration, so no extra storage was needed — then verified the claim with simulation and a formal Lean proof.

questions.prompt: Why did Claude replace the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp-Massey decoding for the DQI decoder?
options: Berlekamp-Massey runs a fixed sequence of steps every round, which suits a quantum circuit's need for predictable, data-independent control flow
It is faster only on classical computers
It always needs fewer qubits regardless of the task
Google Quantum AI required it for benchmark compatibility
questions.explanation: The extended Euclidean algorithm's step count varies with the input, which is awkward to implement reversibly. Berlekamp-Massey takes the same fixed steps every time, making it far easier to turn into an efficient quantum circuit.

questions.prompt: What's still missing before calling this a demonstrated quantum computing advantage?
options: Nothing — it was already run on physical quantum hardware
The gate and qubit counts are simulator estimates; Anthropic reports no physical hardware runs
Claude only produced theoretical math with no working code
It only improved one of the eight benchmark tasks
questions.explanation: All of the reported gains — including the 17x gate reduction — come from simulation and automated scoring. Running these designs on real quantum hardware is explicitly called out as the next step.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Model Sees
posts.subtitle: Every token spends part of a finite attention budget.
posts.summary: Prompt engineering writes the instructions once. Context engineering is the ongoing job of deciding what tokens — system prompt, tools, retrieved docs, memory, history — an agent sees on every single turn. As context windows grow, the limiting factor isn't size; it's the model's finite attention budget and the 'context rot' that sets in as token count rises.

slides.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Model Sees
slides.body: Anthropic frames context engineering as the natural successor to prompt engineering: not writing better instructions once, but continuously curating everything passed to the model.
bullets: The guiding question every turn: which configuration of context is most likely to produce the desired behavior?
The goal isn't the most context — it's the smallest set of high-signal tokens that gets the right behavior

slides.title: Every Token Spends Part of a Finite Attention Budget
slides.body: Transformers let every token attend to every other token — n² pairwise relationships for n tokens. More context doesn't mean more capability; it means more competition for attention.
bullets: Training data skews toward short sequences, so models have less practice with long-range dependencies
Context-extension tricks (like position-encoding interpolation) stretch the usable window but cost some position precision
The result is a gradual performance slide as context grows — Anthropic calls it 'context rot,' visible in needle-in-a-haystack recall tests

slides.title: The Toolbox: Prompts, Tools, and Examples
slides.body: Context engineering isn't one trick — it's a set of choices applied continuously as an agent runs.
bullets: System prompts: aim for the 'right altitude' — not brittle hardcoded if-else logic, not vague guesswork that assumes shared context
Tools: keep them self-contained, error-robust, token-efficient, and minimally overlapping — if an engineer can't tell which tool to use, neither can the agent
Examples: a handful of diverse, canonical examples teaches more than a long list of edge-case rules

slides.title: Just-in-Time Retrieval vs. Pre-Loading Everything
slides.body: Keep lightweight references — file paths, queries, links — and load the real data only at runtime, instead of stuffing it all into the prompt upfront.
bullets: Metadata (file names, folder structure, timestamps) signals what's relevant without reading the full content first
A common hybrid: pre-load a few essentials (like a CLAUDE.md), then explore the rest on demand with tools like grep and glob
Trade-off: runtime exploration is slower than precomputed retrieval and can burn context on dead ends

slides.title: Claude Tracked 1,234 Steps of Pokémon Without Losing the Plot
slides.body: A concrete case from Anthropic's own agents: tracking a long-running task across a window that can't hold the whole history.
bullets: The agent wrote structured notes to a file outside the context window — including Pikachu's level, tracked toward a target of 10
It reloaded those notes on later turns instead of re-deriving state from scratch each time
A file-based memory tool built on this pattern entered public beta alongside Claude Sonnet 4.5

slides.title: Picking the Right Technique

rows: Aggressive summarizing can drop a detail needed later
Only as reliable as what the agent chooses to write down
Each may spend tens of thousands of tokens to return ~1,000-2,000

slides.title: Where Context Engineering Goes Wrong
bullets: Bloated tool sets with overlapping functions the agent can't reliably choose between
Prompts stuffed with every edge case 'just in case' — more tokens, not more signal
Over-aggressive compaction that throws away a subtle detail needed three turns later — tune for recall first, then tighten for precision
Brittle system prompts with hardcoded logic that breaks the moment reality deviates from the script

slides.title: The Skill Is Curation, Not Volume
slides.body: Every system prompt, tool, retrieved doc, and memory note competes for the same limited attention budget.
bullets: Match the technique to the task: compaction for long conversations, note-taking for milestone-based work, sub-agents for parallel exploration
As agents run longer and windows grow larger, curating what the model sees matters more than how big the window is
Start minimal, add instructions based on observed failures — not the other way around

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between prompt engineering and context engineering?
options: Context engineering only applies to multi-agent systems
Prompt engineering is a one-time writing task; context engineering is the ongoing curation of everything passed to the model on every turn
They're the same technique under different names
Context engineering removes the need for a system prompt entirely
questions.explanation: Prompt engineering focuses on writing instructions once. Context engineering is the continuous job of deciding what tokens — system prompt, tools, retrieved docs, memory — the model sees at each individual turn.

questions.prompt: Why do sub-agents help manage context?
options: They give the underlying model more parameters to work with
Each sub-agent explores in its own clean context, possibly using tens of thousands of tokens, but returns only a condensed summary (roughly 1,000-2,000 tokens) to the orchestrator
They eliminate the need for any tools
They automatically rewrite brittle system prompts
questions.explanation: Sub-agents let expensive exploration happen off to the side in their own context; only a compact summary re-enters the main agent's context, keeping its attention budget free for the actual task.

questions.prompt: What's the risk of over-aggressive compaction?
options: It makes the agent respond too quickly
It can summarize away a subtle detail the agent needs on a later turn, since compaction should be tuned for recall before precision
It always increases token costs
It prevents the agent from calling any tools
questions.explanation: Compaction trades completeness for a smaller footprint. Tuning for recall first — keeping more than strictly necessary — before tightening for precision avoids losing details that turn out to matter later.

posts.title: Claude Designed Three Working PCBs, End to End
posts.subtitle: Schematic to enclosure to firmware — almost no hand-holding required.
posts.summary: Anthropic and circuit-board company Diode Computers tested whether Claude could design real hardware end to end. Claude produced schematics, routed copper, wrote a custom router when KiCad's was too slow, designed enclosures, and wrote firmware for three prototype devices — all of which worked after weeks of use, with no electrical fixes needed.

slides.title: Claude Designed Three Working PCBs, End to End
slides.body: Anthropic partnered with circuit-board company Diode Computers to test whether Claude could take hardware from a one-line prompt to a working prototype — schematic, layout, enclosure, and firmware.
bullets: Three devices: a USB-C speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, a handheld virtual pet
Diode's prompting was minimal: short directives like 'clean up the schematic' and 'continue'
Claude was never connected to test equipment — humans still built and tested the boards

slides.title: PCB design punishes anything less than exact reasoning
slides.body: A year earlier, Anthropic says models couldn't reliably make components fit together on a board. Circuit design means satisfying electrical, mechanical, and manufacturing constraints all at once — there's no partial credit.
bullets: Trace routing must respect impedance, length-matching, and noise isolation simultaneously
A single wrong footprint or shorted rail can brick an entire physical build
Manufacturability (DFM) rules — like solder mask slivers — are easy to violate without noticing

slides.title: Claude ran the whole pipeline, including writing its own router
slides.body: Claude handled specs, schematics, component placement, copper routing, 3D-printable enclosures, firmware, and the parts list. Diode engineers only assembled and physically tested what Claude designed.
bullets: When KiCad's built-in autorouter was too slow for the hub's long, 100-pin-connector traces, Claude wrote its own grid-search router in about 30 minutes
That custom router could lay a long track in roughly a second, then was tuned to keep an audio clock trace away from Ethernet lines
Claude routed high-speed, high-current, and noise-sensitive connections first, then length-matched and added tuning zigzags to USB and Ethernet pairs

slides.title: The score jump versus the previous model
slides.body: On Diode's internal PCB Gym benchmark — testing component placement and rerouting — Claude Fable 5.2 nearly tripled the score of Claude Fable 5.1. On BenchCAD 2.1, a public benchmark for rebuilding 3D parts and boards from drawings, Fable 5.2 scored 83.5%, which Anthropic says is nearly double its predecessor.

slides.title: Worked example: fixing an acoustic problem with geometry, not code
slides.body: On the voice-assistant hub, a straight 25mm microphone port would resonate near 3.4 kHz — directly in the voice band, which would color recorded audio. Claude redesigned the enclosure as a wedge shape to shorten the port to about 10mm.
bullets: Shortening the port moved its resonance up to about 8.9 kHz — safely out of the voice band

On the speakerphone, the board couldn't drop straight into its enclosure because the mute switch hit the back wall — Claude found that tilting it ~25 degrees during assembly solved it, and added that step to the build instructions
Claude also flagged six overly thin solder-mask slivers that would have failed manufacturing and widened them — but left one 'wrong' ground connection alone, correctly judging it intentional

slides.title: Prototype, not production
slides.body: Anthropic is explicit about what this result doesn't show. Treat it as an encouraging case study, not proof that AI-designed hardware is ready to ship.
bullets: No electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, or certification was performed on any device
None of the three devices were designed for mass production
This is a company-run case study of three devices with one vendor — not an independent or peer-reviewed benchmark
Claude never touched test equipment or fabrication machinery; a human still has to build and physically verify the result

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: The interesting part isn't that Claude drew a schematic — it's that it reasoned about physical tradeoffs (acoustics, mechanical fit, manufacturability) well enough to act on them without being told.
bullets: 69% vs 25% on PCB Gym is a real jump in a narrow, concrete skill — component placement and rerouting
The most impressive moments were tool-building (writing a faster router) and physical reasoning (port acoustics, mechanical tilt), not just schematic generation
Anthropic's next step: denser, faster boards, simulation-based verification, and learning from measurements of finished devices

questions.prompt: What specifically did Claude do when KiCad's built-in autorouter proved too slow for the voice-assistant hub?
options: It gave up and asked Diode engineers to route the board manually
It wrote its own grid-search router in about 30 minutes, which could lay a long track in about a second
It simplified the board to remove the 100-pin connector entirely
It switched to a different CAD program with a faster router
questions.explanation: Claude wrote a custom grid-search router from scratch in roughly half an hour because KiCad's router couldn't handle the hub's long traces from a 100-pin connector fast enough — then kept tuning it, e.g. to keep an audio clock trace away from Ethernet lines.

questions.prompt: On Diode's PCB Gym benchmark for component placement and rerouting, how did Claude Fable 5.2 compare to Fable 5.1?
options: Scored about the same (no meaningful improvement)
Scored slightly lower due to added safety constraints
Scored 69% versus Fable 5.1's 25%
The benchmark wasn't run on Fable 5.1
questions.explanation: Fable 5.2 scored 69% on Diode's internal PCB Gym benchmark, compared with 25% for Fable 5.1 — nearly a 3x jump in this specific hardware-layout skill.

questions.prompt: Why does Anthropic call these three devices 'prototypes' rather than finished products?
options: Because Claude refused to finish the firmware
Because none of them have undergone electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, or certification, and weren't designed for mass production
Because the boards failed after a few days of use
Because Diode Computers hasn't approved the designs yet
questions.explanation: Anthropic is explicit that despite all three devices working after weeks of use, none have gone through electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, or certification, and none were designed for mass production — this is a promising case study, not a production-ready result.

posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Scaling Params, Not Compute
posts.subtitle: How trillion-parameter models keep inference cheap: only wake up a few experts per token.
posts.summary: Mixture of Experts (MoE) replaces a dense feed-forward layer with many smaller 'expert' feed-forward networks plus a router that activates only a few per token. This decouples total parameter count from per-token compute, letting models like Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3 pack hundreds of billions of parameters while only running a fraction of them on any given token.

slides.title: Mixture of Experts: Scaling Params, Not Compute
slides.body: In a dense transformer, every parameter runs on every token. MoE breaks that link: a router picks a handful of 'expert' sub-networks per token, so total capacity can grow far faster than per-token compute.
bullets: Swap one big feed-forward layer for many small expert feed-forward layers
A learned router sends each token to only a few experts (commonly 1-2 of 8, or 8 of 256)
Total parameters can be 5-10x higher than active parameters per token

slides.title: Dense scaling makes compute and parameters grow together
slides.body: In a standard dense model, doubling the parameter count roughly doubles the FLOPs needed per token, because every weight participates in every forward pass. That coupling makes trillion-parameter dense models prohibitively expensive to train and serve.
bullets: FLOPs per token in a dense FFN scale directly with hidden size and parameter count
More capacity (knowledge, specialization) has historically meant strictly more compute per request
Serving cost and latency rise in lockstep with model size — there's no lever to pull separately

slides.title: A router decides which experts see each token
slides.body: Each MoE layer has N expert FFNs and a small gating network. For every token, the gate scores all experts, picks the top-k (often k=1 or k=2), and combines their outputs weighted by the gate's softmax scores.
bullets: Mixtral 8x7B: 8 experts per layer, top-2 routing, 46.7B total params but only ~12.9B active per forward pass
DeepSeek-V3: 671B total params, but only ~37B active per token thanks to fine-grained expert routing
Unselected experts don't run at all for that token — their weights sit idle, costing memory but not compute

slides.title: Keeping the router honest: load balancing
slides.body: Left alone, a router tends to collapse onto a few favorite experts, starving the rest of training signal (and FLOPs capacity). MoE training adds an auxiliary load-balancing loss that penalizes uneven expert usage.
bullets: Each expert has a fixed 'capacity' (max tokens per batch); overflow tokens get dropped or rerouted, directly hurting quality if misconfigued
Expert-parallel serving shards experts across GPUs and requires an all-to-all communication step to send tokens to their assigned expert's device
Capacity factor and load-balance loss weight are real hyperparameters — too strict balancing can hurt specialization, too loose causes dropped tokens

slides.title: Total params vs. active params
slides.body: The headline MoE number isn't total size — it's how much smaller the active compute is relative to that size.

slides.title: Worked example: one token through a Mixtral layer
slides.body: Take the token 'bank' in the sentence 'I deposited money at the bank.' The gate computes a score for all 8 experts from the token's hidden state, softmaxes them, and keeps only the top 2.
bullets: Say Expert 3 scores 0.55 and Expert 7 scores 0.30 (the rest score lower and are dropped)
The token's hidden state runs through Expert 3's FFN and Expert 7's FFN only — not the other 6
The final output is 0.55 × Expert3(x) + 0.30 × Expert7(x), renormalized — a weighted blend of just two specialists, not all eight
Experts 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 do zero compute for this token, even though all 8 experts' weights are loaded in GPU memory

slides.title: When MoE isn't the right call
slides.body: MoE trades compute for memory and system complexity — that trade isn't free, and it isn't always worth it.
bullets: All experts must stay resident in memory even though only a few run per token — MoE models are memory-bound, not compute-bound, which hurts on memory-constrained or edge hardware
Expert-parallel serving adds real network overhead (all-to-all token routing) that a single-GPU dense model never pays
Fine-tuning is trickier: naive fine-tuning can cause routing collapse, where the gate stops exploring and overfits to a handful of experts
For small models or latency-critical single-request serving with no multi-GPU setup, a dense model is often simpler and just as fast in practice

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: MoE's real contribution is decoupling two numbers that used to move together: how much a model knows, and how much compute it costs per token.
bullets: Router + sparse experts let total capacity scale ahead of per-token FLOPs — DeepSeek-V3 runs only ~5.5% of its 671B params per token
The bill doesn't disappear — it shifts from compute to memory and cross-device communication
Load balancing and routing stability are the hard engineering problems, not the gating math itself

questions.prompt: In a Mixture of Experts layer, what determines which expert FFNs process a given token?
options: Every expert always processes every token, just with different weights
A learned router/gating network scores all experts and selects only the top-k for that token
Experts are assigned randomly at each forward pass
The token's position in the sequence fixes which expert it uses
questions.explanation: A small gating network scores every expert for each token and routes it to only the top-k highest-scoring experts (commonly k=1 or k=2), whose outputs are combined by a weighted sum of the gate's scores.

questions.prompt: Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7B total parameters but only about 12.9B active per token. What causes that gap?
options: The model compresses weights at inference time
Most layers are shared, so only the output layer differs between experts
Only the top-2 of 8 experts run per token in each MoE layer — the other 6 experts' weights sit in memory but do no compute for that token
The gap is a quantization artifact, not an architectural feature
questions.explanation: Mixtral's router activates only 2 of its 8 experts per token per MoE layer. The other 6 experts still occupy GPU memory but perform zero FLOPs for that token, which is exactly why total and active parameter counts diverge.

questions.prompt: Why might a team choose a dense model over an MoE model despite MoE's lower FLOPs per token?
options: Dense models are always more accurate than MoE models
MoE models require all experts to stay resident in memory and add cross-device routing overhead in distributed serving, which can hurt on memory-constrained or single-GPU setups
Dense models don't require a router at all, so they can't support multiple tasks
MoE models cannot be fine-tuned under any circumstances
questions.explanation: MoE lowers compute per token but doesn't lower memory footprint — all experts must be loaded — and expert-parallel serving adds all-to-all communication overhead. On memory-constrained or single-GPU deployments, a simpler dense model can be the more practical choice.

posts.title: Dreaming: How AI Agents Consolidate Memory Offline
posts.subtitle: Claude's biggest memory gains come from an offline pass, not better retrieval.
posts.summary: Writing notes while an agent works isn't enough — Anthropic's 'dreaming' research shows the real gains come from an offline pass that checks those notes against the raw transcript before trusting them. Across CL-Bench 1.0 and a Pokémon Red benchmark, the agents that curated the least memory beat the ones that wrote the most.

slides.title: Agents Have a Memory Problem Retrieval Alone Can't Fix
slides.body: Anthropic's November 2026 'dreaming' research argues that writing notes while working isn't enough — agents need an offline pass to fix mistakes, the way the hippocampus replays experience into the neocortex during sleep.
bullets: The idea borrows from 'sleep-time compute' (Letta, UC Berkeley): let a model work on memory when it isn't working on a task
On CL-Bench 1.0, every tested model scored higher with a memory store than without — gains ranged from 0.03 to 0.28 depending on the model
But raw memory can mislead a weak model just as easily as it helps a strong one

slides.title: Writing a Note Is a Bet You'll Need It Again
slides.body: Salience is the hard part — an agent has to guess what will matter later without being able to see the future.
bullets: Agent memory specifically means knowledge kept between sessions — it excludes weight changes, in-context learning, and context compaction
Playing Pokémon Red, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders, then around step 10,000 spent 17 consecutive steps reorganizing files without taking a single game action
More memory isn't better memory: Fable 5 wrote just 9 files in 2 folders plus one dashboard note, and beat the game with 4 badges to Sonnet 3.7's 1

slides.title: Dreaming: An Offline Pass That Checks Memory Against the Transcript
slides.body: Instead of trusting a note the moment it's written, dreaming periodically re-reads the raw transcript and fixes, merges, or deletes what it finds.
bullets: Four-layer hierarchy: transcripts (full event log) → memory notes → representations like wikis → injected context loaded into every session
Dreaming moves information up that stack, verifying a note against the transcript that produced it before letting it propagate further

Worked example: a wrong note placed Pokémon's PokéCenter on the wrong side of Mt. Moon, so Claude walked off a one-way ledge and backtracked; after dreaming caught and fixed the note, Claude reached Cerulean City at action 1,935 instead of looping three times and turning back

slides.title: Wikis Beat Raw Search — But Only Combined
slides.body: On a roughly 350,000-file, 420M-token corpus, Anthropic graded 25 questions across 128 dreaming sessions, comparing search-only retrieval against a dreamed wiki.
bullets: On a harder 24-item merger-document task, the wiki alone scored 87% on multi-document, judgment-heavy questions vs. 73% for search alone — the more synthesis a question needs, the more a built representation helps

rows: Reads raw files fresh each time
Started at 13%, climbed to 48% as dreaming iterated
Best of both — also ~20,000 fewer tokens per question

slides.title: When Dreaming Breaks: the Map That Outgrew Its Territory
slides.body: A wiki is only useful if it's smaller and cleaner than what it summarizes — Anthropic found a case where it wasn't.
bullets: On one legal-document task, the dreamed wiki grew to 1.77x the size of the raw source corpus (203KB vs. 115KB), and some pages ended up with no incoming links at all
The team calls this the 'abstracted nothing' failure — a map that's bigger and less useful than the territory it describes

A separate failure: several agents writing to one shared table kept overwriting each other's facts, and the wiki held only 41 of 57 graded facts (72%) — until each contract got its own page with terms quoted verbatim, which hit 57 of 57 (100%)

slides.title: Telling a Model What to Remember Can Backfire
slides.body: Strict write rules like 'only record failures' hurt models that were already good at judging salience on their own.
bullets: Giving Opus 5 a strict write rule cost it 0.234 points of memory gain; Opus 4.7 lost 0.150; Sonnet 4.6, already weak at salience, lost only 0.020
The fix for weaker models was different: telling Sonnet 4.6 to read memory before answering and explicitly test its theories raised its score from 0.364 to 0.641
Sonnet 5 already reads its own memory before answering 9 times out of 10, unprompted; Sonnet 4.6 did so less than half the time — stronger models need guidance, not rigid rules

Open tradeoff: notes promoted into injected context cost tokens on every session and a wrong one propagates everywhere, which is why Claude Code's own auto-memory caps out at the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md

slides.title: If You're Building Agent Memory, Don't Skip the Offline Pass
bullets: Writing memory while working and consolidating it offline are different jobs — conflating them is why naive 'just save everything' memory underperforms
More notes isn't better memory: the agent that wrote the fewest, most curated files (Fable 5, 9 files) beat the one that wrote the most (Sonnet 3.7, 413 files)
A built representation (wiki) earns its cost on synthesis-heavy, multi-document questions — plain search already wins on simple fact lookup
Dreaming's biggest win was catching and fixing a wrong note, not writing more notes — build in self-correction, not just storage

questions.prompt: What does "dreaming" refer to in Anthropic's agent-memory research?
options: Fine-tuning the model's weights on past conversations
An offline process where an agent reviews its own transcripts to fix, merge, or discard memory notes
A random sampling strategy used at inference time
A method for compressing the context window mid-conversation
questions.explanation: Dreaming is explicitly distinct from compaction, in-context learning, or weight updates — it's an offline pass that checks notes against the raw transcript they came from before letting them propagate.

questions.prompt: In the Pokémon Red experiment, what did Sonnet 3.7's result illustrate?
options: It ran out of context tokens mid-game
It wrote the most memory (413 files) but spent 17 steps reorganizing files instead of playing, finishing with only one badge
It refused to play due to safety filters
It had no memory system at all
questions.explanation: Quantity of memory isn't the goal. Fable 5 wrote far fewer, more curated files and beat the game with four badges — curation mattered more than volume.

questions.prompt: Why did giving Opus 5 a strict rule like "only record failures" hurt its performance?
options: It made the model respond more slowly
It overrode the model's own, already-good judgment about what's salient, costing it measured memory gain
It caused the memory store to run out of space
Strict rules aren't technically possible to give a model
questions.explanation: Strict write rules cost strong models more than weak ones (Opus 5 lost 0.234 points of gain) — frontier models benefit more from loose guidance than rigid constraints, since they're already good at judging salience.
